title: Output credentials cross proxy boundaries only inside the WebSocket protocol
context: CHG-0045 established one exact-Show, read-only and immediately rotatable Output authority, but the issued browser-source URL placed its bearer in the HTTP query and the client copied it into the WebSocket request target. HTTP and WebSocket request targets are routinely observable at TLS terminators and access-log boundaries. The client also defaulted to a build-time plaintext ws://localhost endpoint, so serving the same bundle through HTTPS did not produce a same-origin WSS connection. RFC 3986 separates URI fragments before dereference, while RFC 6455 permits application messages only after the WebSocket opening handshake. A TLS proxy experiment against the prior order would therefore reproduce credential-bearing request targets and mixed-content configuration rather than test a safe deployment boundary.
decision: A newly issued Output URL carries its bearer only in a client-side URI fragment. The browser output reads that fragment locally and sends the bearer as a bounded authenticate.output application message immediately after the WebSocket connection opens and before any subscription or other message. The server never authenticates an Output from an HTTP or WebSocket request target, rejects non-authentication traffic from an unauthenticated browser connection, and closes an unauthenticated connection after a bounded deadline. Successful Output authentication installs the exact Show authority established by ADR-0004 and CHG-0045; rotation retires the established socket as before. The browser WebSocket endpoint defaults to /ws on the page's own origin, mapping HTTPS pages to WSS and HTTP pages to WS, while an explicit build-time endpoint remains available for exceptional split-origin deployments. Query-bearing legacy Output URLs fail closed and require credential rotation. Secure proxy guidance keeps both public HTTP and WebSocket endpoints on the same verified HTTPS origin, keeps OverlayKit upstream listeners on loopback, preserves Origin validation, and excludes WebSocket payload capture from operational logging. This decision proves only standards-based browser transport and a local TLS-termination boundary; it does not establish execution in OBS, public certificate or DNS operation, hostile-network resilience beyond verified TLS, external proxy products, network-loss recovery, or operator perception.
consequences: HTTP page requests and WebSocket upgrade request targets generated by OverlayKit no longer contain the Output bearer.
The server must admit a short-lived unauthenticated browser WebSocket state and fail it closed before any subscription authority exists.
The client must authenticate before initial subscription and before restoring subscriptions after reconnect.
A production output bundle can derive wss://<output-origin>/ws without embedding a deployment hostname at build time.
Previously issued query-token URLs stop authenticating and the Owner must rotate and replace them.
Access logs may retain ordinary request metadata, but operators must not enable WebSocket frame or payload capture because the authentication frame contains the bearer.
A standards-compliant branded-Chrome proof remains evidence about the web transport boundary, not evidence that an OBS process captured or composited the result.

policies.statement: OverlayKit-generated Output page and WebSocket request targets must not contain an Output bearer; query-string Output authentication is rejected.
An Output connection must authenticate through one bounded application message before it may subscribe, ping, mutate, or receive production state.
Every reconnect must authenticate the page-held credential before restoring subscriptions, so an old credential cannot inherit later ambient authority.
Absent an explicit endpoint, the browser output must derive /ws from its page origin and select WSS whenever the page uses HTTPS.
Local TLS termination and branded-browser evidence must not be represented as real OBS, public PKI, external proxy, hostile-network, network-loss, capture-quality, or operator-perception evidence.
